document.title: "When and why the decision to send troops was made"
document.authors: Georgy M. Kornienko (memoir, The Cold War: Testimony of a Participant)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
document.note: Excerpt from the memoirs of Georgy Kornienko, top deputy to Foreign Minister Gromyko, giving an insider view of Gromyko's thinking and Soviet decision-making on Afghanistan in 1979, and pointing to October 1979 as the turning point in Gromyko's thinking about Amin.

events.description: Ustinov orally ordered General Staff to prepare one paratrooper division, five military-transport aviation divisions, readiness of two motorized rifle divisions, and pontoon regiment staffing.
Final political decision to send troops made by Brezhnev, Suslov, Andropov, Ustinov and Gromyko.
Ustinov announced decision to Defense Ministry leadership; directive signed to send contingents into Afghanistan.
Gromyko and Kornienko repeatedly discuss and reject Afghan requests for Soviet troops.
American military ships stationed in the Persian Gulf and reports of a possible US invasion of Iran push Ustinov to favor sending troops.
Ustinov orally orders the General Staff to prepare paratroop and transport aviation divisions and raise readiness of motorized rifle divisions in the Turkestan Military District.
Final political decision to send Soviet troops into Afghanistan by Brezhnev, Suslov, Andropov, Ustinov and Gromyko; Politburo resolution drawn up afterwards.
Ustinov announces the troop decision to Defense Ministry leadership; the first directive signed by the Defense Minister is prepared.

sources_cited: Georgy M. Kornienko, The Cold War: Testimony of a Participant, Moscow, 1994
key_claims: Gromyko and Kornienko agreed through October 1979 that sending troops to Afghanistan was impermissible.
Ustinov likely first shifted toward intervention, prompted by US naval deployments in the Persian Gulf and fears of an invasion of Iran.
Andropov was influenced by KGB portrayals of Amin as an American agent and exaggerated Soviet ability to shape events.
The General Staff leadership (Ogarkov, Akhromeev, Varennikov) objected on professional grounds but was overridden.
The decision was made on 12 Dec 1979 by Brezhnev, Suslov, Andropov, Ustinov and Gromyko, not the full Politburo.
A Politburo resolution was prepared after the fact and signed by almost all members.
